cards.title: Can DynFO maintain the parity of vertices covered by red predecessors?
cards.formal: Does there exist a DynFO program that maintains the Boolean query |{y∈D:∃x∈D (R(x)∧E(x,y))}|≡1 mod 2 under arbitrary single-tuple insertions and deletions in a directed edge relation E⊆D² and a red-vertex relation R⊆D? Use one fixed finite auxiliary relational vocabulary and fixed first-order update formulas for every finite domain D. All input and auxiliary relations are empty initially, and there are no built-in order or arithmetic relations. The program must be correct after every finite sequence of updates, with no bound on the length of that sequence.
cards.why: Would clarify whether first-order dynamic maintenance can express a basic combination of existential coverage and parity counting, beyond the already understood parity of a directly stored set.

cards.definitions: The domain D is a fixed finite set throughout a run; updates do not create or delete vertices. An element y is covered when at least one red predecessor x has an arc x→y. A covered vertex is counted once, regardless of how many red predecessors it has, and it need not itself be red. E is a binary relation, so loops are allowed; R is unary. The four update types are ins_E(u,v), del_E(u,v), ins_R(u), and del_R(u). Insertions of present tuples and deletions of absent tuples leave the input relation unchanged and are also allowed. A program chooses finitely many auxiliary relation symbols S, each of a fixed finite arity, including a distinguished zero-ary answer bit Ans. For each S and update type δ it supplies a first-order formula φ_{S,δ}(p̄;z̄), where p̄ are the changed tuple’s parameters and z̄ has the arity of S. The formula may use equality, the current input and auxiliary relations, Boolean connectives, and quantification over individual domain elements. It has no parity/counting quantifier, quantification over sets, function symbol or built-in numeric relation. After update δ(ā), each auxiliary relation becomes {b̄:(I,A)⊨φ_{S,δ}(ā;b̄)}, evaluated on the old input I and old auxiliary state A. All auxiliary updates occur simultaneously, alongside the specified input change. Empty initialization makes Ans false, correctly answering the empty covered set. The program’s formulas and arities are independent of |D| and of the update history. The number and arities of auxiliary relations are unrestricted finite constants chosen by the program; thus it may use polynomially many auxiliary bits, with its own fixed polynomial exponent. DynFO measures expressibility of these updates, rather than sequential constant-time execution of a formula on a Turing machine.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer is a finite collection of first-order update formulas and a proof of correctness from empty initialization for every finite domain and every finite update sequence. A negative answer must show that every such program, allowing arbitrary fixed auxiliary arities, fails on some domain and sequence. A lower bound only for quantifier-free formulas or a fixed arity, a program requiring unrestricted initial advice, or an algorithm for a bounded-degree variant does not settle the stated DynFO question.

context_blocks.title: Coverage makes a simple parity question harder
context_blocks.text: Parity of a directly stored unary set can be maintained by tracking individual membership changes. Here a red-vertex update can change the coverage of many successors, while overlapping red neighborhoods mean that not every incident successor actually changes status. The queried parity concerns covered vertices, not the number of red vertices or red incident edges.

context_blocks.title: The source separates quantifier-free and quantified updates
context_blocks.text: The paper proves that ParityExists cannot be maintained with quantifier-free first-order update rules, even with stronger initialization allowances. Its open question permits full first-order quantification and auxiliary relations of any fixed finite arity, so that lower bound is insufficient.

context_blocks.title: Degree-filtered queries admit positive results
context_blocks.text: The source studies the variant counting only covered vertices whose indegree is at most a threshold. It proves DynFO results when the threshold grows logarithmically, with the stated built-in order/BIT conventions and an active-domain version without them. This is a filtered counting query, not a solution of unrestricted ParityExists.

context_blocks.title: A benchmark for dynamic counting expressibility
context_blocks.text: The query has the form of a parity quantifier outside an existential quantifier. Understanding it is a basic obstacle to classifying which queries from first-order logic with parity can be maintained by ordinary first-order updates. Solving this one query alone is not asserted to settle that broader inclusion.

cards.context:
Parity of a directly stored unary set can be maintained by tracking individual membership changes. Here a red-vertex update can change the coverage of many successors, while overlapping red neighborhoods mean that not every incident successor actually changes status. The queried parity concerns covered vertices, not the number of red vertices or red incident edges.

The paper proves that ParityExists cannot be maintained with quantifier-free first-order update rules, even with stronger initialization allowances. Its open question permits full first-order quantification and auxiliary relations of any fixed finite arity, so that lower bound is insufficient.

The source studies the variant counting only covered vertices whose indegree is at most a threshold. It proves DynFO results when the threshold grows logarithmically, with the stated built-in order/BIT conventions and an active-domain version without them. This is a filtered counting query, not a solution of unrestricted ParityExists.

The query has the form of a parity quantifier outside an existential quantifier. Understanding it is a basic obstacle to classifying which queries from first-order logic with parity can be maintained by ordinary first-order updates. Solving this one query alone is not asserted to settle that broader inclusion.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
